props.title: Dear Frankie

sections.content: Dear Frankie stands among the most tender Scottish dramas ever made, anchored by Emily Mortimer's heartbreaking performance as Lizzie, a single mother protecting her deaf son through elaborate letters supposedly from his absent father. The film shares emotional DNA with other intimate Scottish character studies like Sweet Sixteen (2002) and Red Road (2006), but brings a uniquely delicate touch to working-class Glasgow life. Director Shona Auerbach crafts scenes with remarkable restraint, letting small gestures and unspoken moments carry tremendous emotional weight.

sections.content: The film belongs to a powerful subset of parental deception dramas, where lies told out of love create complex moral dilemmas. Like Life is Beautiful (1997), where a father shields his son from Holocaust horrors through elaborate fiction, or The Farewell (2019), where a family conceals a terminal diagnosis, Dear Frankie explores how protecting loved ones sometimes means constructing alternate realities. Gerard Butler's nuanced performance as "the stranger" hired to play Frankie's father adds layers of complexity to these themes of truth, identity and sacrifice.

What sets Dear Frankie apart is its immersive portrayal of Frankie's world through sound design and visual storytelling. The film's approach to depicting deafness shares creative DNA with Sound of Metal (2019) and Children of a Lesser God (1986), but focuses more on emotional rather than literal silence. Jack McElhone's remarkable performance as Frankie captures both the isolation and rich inner life of a child processing the world differently. SUBHEAD: The Power of Written Words

sections.content: The letters at the heart of Dear Frankie elevate it beyond typical family drama territory. Like 84 Charing Cross Road (1987) and The Lake House (2006), the film uses written correspondence to explore deep emotional connections formed through words alone. Lizzie's letters, creating an entire world of seafaring adventures for Frankie's fictional father, echo the imaginative power of films like Big Fish (2003), where storytelling becomes an act of love.
